title: Chinese Military Distills US AI for Battlefield Systems, Pentagon's $59B PAC-3 Deal Rests on Congress, India's First Indigenous Turbojet Engine
subhead: A Reuters investigation reveals Chinese PLA researchers systematically extracting capabilities from OpenAI and Anthropic models for military AI, the Pentagon signs a record $59B interceptor contract that Congress hasn't funded, and India achieves a domestic propulsion milestone previously mastered by only a handful of nations.

sections.heading: Chinese PLA Researchers Use US AI Models to Build Battlefield Systems
sections.body:
A Reuters review of more than 80 Chinese academic papers and patents found that military-linked researchers in China have systematically used 'model distillation' — extracting capabilities from leading US AI models — to train domestic systems for battlefield operations, surveillance, cyber warfare, and content monitoring. The Jamestown Foundation's Sunny Cheung, who analyzed over 60 of the papers, described it as a coordinated effort to transfer 'expensive, proprietary reasoning from Western models into smaller systems they can control and deploy locally.'

One paper from PLA Unit 96941, a Chinese military intelligence and cyber warfare unit, described using OpenAI's GPT-3.5 to analyze military software code before transferring that knowledge into a domestically developed AI model capable of operating entirely within Chinese military networks. Other research described using Anthropic's Claude to generate training data for social media monitoring systems. Additional studies outlined deploying distilled AI models on drones, autonomous ships, and unmanned submarines during simulated maritime operations.

Anthropic stated it does not provide commercial access to Claude in China and has systems to detect policy violations. OpenAI did not respond to Reuters' request for comment. The findings sharpen the debate over AI governance ahead of US-China talks on the issue.
sections.whyItMatters: Model distillation erodes the effectiveness of US export controls on AI technology — China doesn't need to import chips or frontier models when it can extract their reasoning capabilities through intermediate outputs. This creates a new category of proliferation risk that existing regulatory frameworks weren't designed to address.

sections.heading: Pentagon's Record $59B PAC-3 Deal — Production Promises Only Congress Can Keep
sections.body:
The US Army awarded Lockheed Martin a $53.86 billion contract modification for PAC-3 MSE interceptors, bringing the total seven-year contract value to $58.62 billion, the company and Army announced last week. Separately, L3Harris Technologies signed framework agreements with the Pentagon to nearly triple PAC-3 MSE propulsion production and quadruple THAAD propulsion output over the next seven years.

But a Forbes analysis reveals a critical caveat: these framework agreements are legally non-binding and dependent on congressional funding that has not yet been appropriated. The White House requested $11.4 billion in THAAD procurement for FY2027, of which $10.5 billion relies on budget reconciliation — a process far from guaranteed. For PAC-3 MSE, $10.9 billion of the $12.2 billion request depends on reconciliation. The House Appropriations Committee has approved PAC-3 MSE procurement funding but recommended roughly $174 million less for THAAD than the White House requested through regular appropriations.

Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael Duffey called the deals 'a decisive win for the Warfighter,' but the production increases require massive taxpayer investment at a time when a majority of Americans across every age group oppose both Iran War spending and the trillion-dollar-plus military budget, according to a recent poll.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between Pentagon framework agreements and actual congressional appropriations is where munitions production plans go to die. With PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptors already depleted by roughly two-thirds during the Iran war, the industrial base can scale only if Congress funds it — and that political calculus is far from certain.

sections.heading: India Achieves First Indigenous Expendable Turbojet Engine Milestone
sections.body:
India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has developed the country's first indigenous expendable turbojet engine in the 350 kg thrust class, produced in partnership with Hyderabad-based Azad Engineering. The engine — designed by DRDO's Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE) — can power next-generation cruise missiles and jet-powered kamikaze drones, technology previously mastered by only a handful of nations.

The development marks a significant milestone for India's aerospace propulsion base, which has long depended on foreign engines for its missile and UAV programs. Janes confirmed the achievement, noting it opens the door to domestically powered long-range strike weapons rather than relying on imported Russian or Israeli propulsion systems.

India has been accelerating its indigenous defense manufacturing push under the 'Make in India' framework, but aero-engine technology has remained one of the hardest domains to localize. The GTRE turbojet, while expendable (single-use), addresses a critical gap in India's ability to produce affordable, high-volume propulsion for loitering munitions and cruise missiles at scale.
sections.whyItMatters: Expendable turbojet capability is the engine behind mass-produceable cruise missiles and kamikaze drones — the dominant weapons of the current era. India's breakthrough reduces its dependence on foreign suppliers for the kind of high-volume, low-cost precision weapons that Ukraine has shown determine battlefield outcomes.

sections.heading: UK Picks Tekever AR5 to Replace Troubled Watchkeeper Fleet in £400M Deal
sections.body:
The UK Ministry of Defence has selected the Portuguese-made Tekever AR5 to succeed the troubled Thales Watchkeeper program, confirming a £400 million ($530 million) deal. The twin-engine AR5 can carry up to 50kg of surveillance equipment and offers longer flight times than the Watchkeeper fleet it replaces.

The Watchkeeper program, the British Army's largest ever UAV procurement, has been a persistent disappointment. According to Janes, it saw only brief operational service at the end of the Afghanistan conflict and was used to track refugee boats in the English Channel in 2020. At least seven Watchkeeper airframes were lost in incidents. The platform's operational availability and cost-effectiveness were repeatedly questioned.

The selection, made under Project Corvus, reflects a wider shift in military drone procurement toward sovereignty and domestic production integration. Shephard Media noted that Tekever's Stormshroud variant — combining the AR3 tactical UAS with Leonardo UK's BriteStorm stand-in jammer — creates an aircrewed platform capable of suppression of enemy air defense (SEAD) operations alongside RAF fighter jets, adding an electronic warfare dimension beyond pure ISR.
sections.whyItMatters: The Watchkeeper saga — years of underperformance and lost airframes — is a cautionary tale about over-engineered European drone programs. The AR5 selection signals that the UK is prioritizing operational availability and cost-effectiveness over domestic industrial protection, and that smaller allied nations can win major NATO contracts when incumbents fail to deliver.

sections.heading: Singapore Enters GCAP Exploratory Talks as Sixth-Gen Fighter Market Consolidates
sections.body:
Singapore has begun early exploratory discussions on possible involvement in the Global Combat Air Programme, according to Janes, making it the latest nation to express interest in the UK-Italy-Japan sixth-generation fighter project. The talks come one week after Canada joined GCAP as its first observer nation on July 21.

Singapore's approach is characteristically deliberate. The Republic of Singapore Air Force currently operates 40 F-15SGs and 49 F-16C/Ds, with 12 F-35Bs and 8 F-35As on order but not yet delivered. Singapore spent years as a Security Cooperative Participant in the F-35 program before placing its first order in 2020, and The War Zone's Roy Choo noted that any GCAP involvement 'is unlikely to transition into a program of record for at least another two decades.'

The GCAP programme recently secured a £4.6 billion ($6.14 billion) contract awarded to industry joint venture Edgewing, and the CEO confirmed the 2035 in-service target will not change even if new countries join. Germany and Saudi Arabia have also expressed interest in joining, the latter a potentially contentious addition given human rights concerns from existing partners.
sections.whyItMatters: Singapore's interest is a signal that the sixth-generation fighter market is consolidating around two programs — GCAP and the US Next Generation Air Dominance — and nations that delay risk being locked out of the only exportable options. With FCAS collapsed, GCAP is becoming the default non-American sixth-gen path.

sections.heading: Baltic Defense Startups Fill Gaps Traditional Contractors Can't Reach
sections.body:
A growing ecosystem of defense technology startups in Lithuania, Estonia, and Latvia is producing precision guidance systems, drone imaging, and autonomous systems designed for the kind of warfare Ukraine has proven decisive. Lithuanian startup Pdkinematics builds guidance systems that help drones strike accurately even when GPS is jammed, with technology already supplied to Ukraine and its European allies. Luna Robotics develops advanced imaging systems for FPV drones.

The Baltic states have some of NATO's highest defence spending levels relative to GDP, with Lithuania allocating 5.3% — the highest among all 32 alliance members. The Lithuanian Armed Forces now provide monthly access to training areas and airspace for emerging technology testing, and the war in Ukraine has given these companies real-world feedback on performance against Russian forces.

Reuters separately reported that military drones straying into the airspace of Finland, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are stoking concerns that the Ukraine war is spilling over into NATO's northern borders, adding urgency to the region's investment in counter-drone and drone technologies. Latvia and Ukraine are also opening a drone factory right on Latvia's border with Russia.
sections.whyItMatters: The Baltics are building what might be called a 'porcupine innovation corridor' — small, agile companies producing the kind of cheap, scalable, GPS-denial-capable systems that legacy contractors struggle to deliver. With Lithuania spending 5.3% of GDP on defence, these startups have both the threat environment and the funding to iterate faster than traditional primes.

sections.heading: German Arms Exports to Israel Surge to €800M, Over 60% for Submarine Project
sections.body:
Germany quietly approved nearly €800 million ($913 million) in military export licenses to Israel during the first five months of 2026 — more than the total value approved during the previous 20 months combined, according to the German government's own figures. Over 60% of the approved licenses are allocated to an unnamed maritime project, which analysts believe refers to the INS Drakon, a German-built Dolphin II-class submarine reportedly delivered to the Israeli Navy last week.

Anadolu Agency noted that the surge marks a sharp escalation in Germany's defense relationship with Israel, even as Berlin has publicly criticized Israeli military actions. Tehran Times described the policy as opaque, while the Al Jazeera report emphasized that German criticism of Israel has not been matched by any reduction in arms exports.

The submarine project specifically raises questions about Germany's willingness to provide strategic underwater capability — the Dolphin-class boats are widely understood to carry nuclear-capable cruise missiles — even during a period of public diplomatic tension.
sections.whyItMatters: Germany's submarine exports to Israel represent the most strategically sensitive category of arms transfer in existence: second-strike nuclear capability platforms. The €800M figure reveals that Berlin's public criticism of Israel and its private arms exports operate on entirely separate tracks, a pattern that undermines German credibility on arms control advocacy.

bottomLine: This week's defense developments expose three structural tensions: the US-China AI race has a new front — model distillation lets China bypass chip export controls by extracting reasoning from frontier models; the Pentagon is writing production promises (Lockheed's $59B PAC-3 deal, L3Harris framework agreements) that only Congress can fund, and congressional appetite is far from guaranteed; and Germany's €800M in arms licenses to Israel shows that strategic submarine exports proceed regardless of political rhetoric. Meanwhile, India's indigenous turbojet engine and the UK's pivot from Watchkeeper to Tekever illustrate two different paths to solving capability gaps — one through homegrown development, the other through pragmatic procurement from smaller allies. The Baltics are quietly building the drone-defense corridor that Ukraine has shown is the future of territorial defense.
sources: Reuters, Forbes, Breaking Defense, Janes, The Aviationist, The War Zone, Shephard Media, Defense Daily, AP News, Stripes, Anadolu Agency, Al Jazeera, Tehran Times, Times of India, Swarajya, Malay Mail/AFP, MSN, Yahoo News, The Bulletin of Atomic Scientists, Independent, India Today, Seeking Alpha
